candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)-Bacterial Soft Rot Erwinia | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Small, water-soaked areas appear and rapidly enlarge, with tissue becoming soft and mushy. An offensive odor usually is present. The soft-rot bacterium, Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora (syn. = Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum), enters through growth cracks or wounds. Prolonged moisture and mild temperatures encourage disease development. Management: avoid overhead irrigation, harvest during dry conditions, avoid wounding plants, storage below 3.9C.

candidate_sources.title: Pectobacterium carotovorum (bacterial soft rot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Pectobacterium carotovorum can cause soft rot on a wide range of crops worldwide, especially in countries with warm and humid climates. The bacteria survives in soil and crop residues, and enters the crop through wounds caused by tools, insects, hail damage or natural openings. It becomes a major problem during wet weather and warm temperatures of 25-30C.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Soft Rot | Scouting Guides for Problems of Vegetables (University of Kentucky)
candidate_sources.snippet: Water-soaked spots initially form, enlarge and become sunken and soft, with plant tissues beneath the spots becoming mushy and discolored. Under severe infection, leaves, stems and roots may rot entirely with a strong odor. Caused by Pectobacterium carotovorum (syn. Erwinia carotovora). Scouting guide with symptoms, conditions favoring disease, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial soft rot of cabbage (2024) | University of Arizona Agricultural IPM
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial soft rot of cabbage caused by Erwinia/Pectobacterium. Small water-soaked areas rapidly enlarge, tissue becomes soft and mushy, an offensive odor is present, and inside the head tissues may liquefy. Management through cultural practices, irrigation control, and avoiding wounding.

candidate_sources.title: Black Rot of Brassicas | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot, caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, is the most important disease of brassica crops worldwide. Characteristic symptoms are V-shaped chlorotic to necrotic lesions extending from the leaf margins and blackening of vascular tissues.

candidate_sources.title: Brassicas, Black Rot : Vegetable : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot of brassicas is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. Leaf infections result in a small, wilted, V-shaped infected area that extends inward from the leaf edge toward the midrib; veins turn black. The bacterium is seedborne and overwinters in plant refuse.

candidate_sources.title: Black Rot of Cole Crops (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot of cole crops is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. Infected lower leaves of cabbage and cauliflower are stunted, turn yellow to brown, wilt, and drop prematurely; veins turn black. The black rot pathogen develops fastest during warm (80 to 95F) and moist conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Practical and Comprehensive Diagnostic Guide for Black Rot of Brassicas | Plant Health Progress (APS)
candidate_sources.snippet: A diagnostic guide for black rot of brassicas caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris (Xcc), describing V-shaped chlorotic to necrotic marginal lesions and blackening of vascular tissue, with diagnostic and management guidance.

candidate_sources.title: Black Rot of Crucifers | Integrated Pest Management | University of Connecticut
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot of crucifers, caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, is a destructive disease of cabbage and other crucifer crops. Management includes hot water seed treatment, crop rotation away from crucifers for at least three years, and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Clubroot of Crucifers | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Clubroot of crucifers, caused by Plasmodiophora brassicae, produces club-shaped galls on the roots of cabbage and other brassicas, blocking absorption of water and nutrients and causing wilting, stunting, and yellowing of shoots.

candidate_sources.title: Clubroot | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Clubroot is caused by the parasitic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, an obligate parasite that develops only in living host cells. All members of the cabbage family are susceptible. The typical symptom is club-shaped galls on the roots, with wilting, stunting, yellowing and redness in advanced stages.

candidate_sources.title: Clubroot of Brassicas | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Clubroot of brassicas is caused by the soilborne pathogen Plasmodiophora brassicae. Infection of fibrous-rooted cole crops (broccoli, cabbage) results in a mass of coral-shaped galls; resting spores can survive in soil for years. Includes symptoms, disease cycle, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Clubroot of Crucifers | University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Clubroot of crucifers, caused by Plasmodiophora brassicae, infects roots of cabbage and related crops, producing swollen, knobbly galls and resting spores that persist in soil. Management includes liming to raise soil pH, sanitation, and resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Downy Mildew on Brassica Crops | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew on brassica crops is caused by the oomycete Hyaloperonospora parasitica. Symptoms on older leaves appear as small, angular, light green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface; gray to white masses of spores develop on the leaf undersurface. The disease does best with high humidity, fog, drizzling rains, and heavy dew.

candidate_sources.title: Brassicas, Downy Mildew : Vegetable : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Peronospora parasitica (= Hyaloperonospora parasitica) overwinters in roots or on leaves/stems of infected living plants. Symptoms include angular yellow lesions on upper leaf surfaces and downy gray-white sporulation underneath. Nearly all cultivated plants and weeds in the Brassicaceae are susceptible; seedlings are more susceptible than older plants.

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)-Downy Mildew (Staghead) | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew (staghead) of cabbage and cauliflower caused by Hyaloperonospora parasitica. Leaf wetness of 4-6 hours at 20Â°C is needed for significant infection. Includes cultural and chemical management recommendations and a fungicide table for the Pacific Northwest.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Cabbage downy mildew (192) - Lucid Apps (Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds)
candidate_sources.snippet: Cabbage downy mildew, caused by Peronospora parasitica (Hyaloperonospora parasitica). Common on cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, broccoli, kale, and kohlrabi. Seedling cotyledons develop discolored necrotic lesions; older leaves show angular yellow lesions with downy growth beneath. Management includes crop rotation, sanitation, and seed treatment.

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)-Phytophthora Root Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora root rot of cabbage and cauliflower. Leaf margins discolor, turn brown, and die; aboveground portions wilt. Lateral roots are absent or decayed and tap roots show dark lesions. Caused by Phytophthora species; favored by wet soil. Management: plant on well-drained soil, avoid excessive irrigation, rotate with nonsusceptible crops.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Root Rot / Cole Crops / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora megasperma survives as resistant spores in soil and infects hosts with swimming zoospores under wet conditions when temperatures range from 55 to 77Â°F. Leaves turn red/purple then yellow before drying; roots become blackened internally and externally with an unpleasant odor. All crucifer crops are susceptible. Plant on well-drained soil and practice a 3-year rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora root rot on Brassica
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora root rot on Brassica. Symptomatic plants are found in wet areas of the field; lateral roots are decayed and tap roots show large dark lesions along their length. CABI Plantwise knowledge bank datasheet covering symptoms, pathogen, and management of Phytophthora root rot of brassicas.
